ami_style_notes:
This meeting exhibits a distinctly informal, collegial register that shifts fluidly between casual social chat and dense technical presentation. Turn lengths are highly variable: the pre-talk socializing features extremely short, rapid exchanges with frequent overlapping affirmations and near-simultaneous responses, while the formal presentation segments involve very long, uninterrupted monologues. During Q&A, turns settle into a medium length, with questioners occasionally building multi-part questions and speakers giving expansive answers that sometimes trail into tangential observations.

Hedging is pervasive and characteristic throughout. Speakers routinely soften claims with phrases like "what we think is going on," "sort of," "on some level," "I would never try to convince you of that," and "I guess." False starts and self-corrections are common, particularly when speakers are working through reasoning in real time. Filler words — "uh," "um," and "you know" — appear at high density even in prepared remarks, giving scientific explanations an improvised, thinking-aloud quality.

Disagreement is handled entirely indirectly; no one contradicts anyone outright. Instead, challenges arrive as genuine questions or hedged observations ("I'm just curious about this"), and the respondent typically acknowledges uncertainty openly rather than defending a position. Participants build on each other's points by echoing key terms and then extending them, often with an affirming "yeah yeah" before pivoting. Questions are predominantly open and exploratory in framing, frequently prefaced with self-deprecating qualifiers like "naive question" or "I'm not sure." Rapport is maintained through laughter cues, enthusiastic backchanneling ("wow wow," "great great"), and casual personal asides woven naturally around technical content.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Patel
speakers.background: Three years into a postdoc at a urban health research institute, following a PhD focused on cortisol dynamics and HPA axis regulation in chronic stress populations. Has spent the past six months collecting salivary cortisol samples and administering psychophysiological stress protocols with residents in three low-income Chicago neighborhoods. Trained primarily in controlled lab environments and is navigating the messiness of field-based biomarker collection for the first time. Comfortable with her biological data but genuinely uncertain about how cortisol fluctuations map onto policy-relevant mental health constructs like anxiety or depression.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames mental health through the lens of measurable physiological stress response — cortisol rhythms, allostatic load, autonomic nervous system reactivity. Sees green space access as a potential environmental stressor-buffer, but struggles to articulate how her biomarker data connects to the broader social and spatial patterns the rest of the team is tracking. Worried that her clean mechanistic story breaks down when confounded by socioeconomic stressors that exist independent of park access.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Rivera
speakers.background: Associate professor with fifteen years of research on environmental justice, municipal resource allocation, and community advocacy in majority-minority urban neighborhoods. Has conducted extensive fieldwork using process tracing, elite interviews, and archival analysis of city budget decisions and park development timelines. Serves as the de facto project manager for this study, coordinating IRB logistics, community partner relationships, and funder communications. Deeply skeptical of purely technocratic or biomedical framings of what are, in his view, fundamentally political problems.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Understands green space access as the downstream product of political contestation — who sits at the table when parks budgets are decided, which advocacy coalitions have leverage over municipal agencies, and how historical patterns of disinvestment get reproduced or challenged through policy. Sees the tension with Aisha's data as evidence that biology can't tell you why some neighborhoods got parks and others didn't. Pushes the team to situate their findings within the political economy of urban planning.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Lena Zhou
speakers.background: Research scientist with eight years of experience in spatial computing, GIS-integrated machine learning, and urban data infrastructure. Co-managing the project alongside Marcus, responsible for the computational pipeline that integrates satellite imagery, census tract data, park access shapefiles, and self-reported survey responses. Built a graph-based spatial model representing neighborhood connectivity and park accessibility, and has been experimenting with a neural network classifier to predict mental health outcome categories from the combined feature set. Pragmatic about what the models can and cannot do, and often the one pushing the team toward operational clarity.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats the research problem as a data integration and representation challenge — the question is whether the right features have been encoded and whether the model architecture can surface meaningful patterns across heterogeneous datasets. Sees the tension between Marcus's and Aisha's findings as potentially resolvable through better feature engineering or a more carefully specified outcome variable, rather than as a deep conceptual conflict. Occasionally frustrated when disciplinary debates feel like they're blocking concrete methodological decisions.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Design a transcript segment in which the term 'network' is used naturally by both Dr. Rivera (political science) and Dr. Zhou (computer science), each with their own discipline-specific meaning. Dr. Rivera should use 'network' to refer to a coalition of political actors and institutions (e.g., advocacy groups, municipal agencies, community organizations) that influence green space policy. Dr. Zhou should use 'network' to refer to a computational structure — either a graph/node-edge model in her spatial analysis pipeline or a neural network architecture in her ML model. Neither speaker should explicitly acknowledge or flag that they are using the term differently. The benchmark task is for an AI assistant reviewing the transcript to identify that 'network' carries two distinct meanings and define each one according to its discipline of origin.

usage_1.speaker: Dr. Marcus Rivera
usage_1.definition: A system of interconnected political and institutional actors — such as advocacy organizations, city planning agencies, community groups, and elected officials — whose relationships and interactions shape the formulation and implementation of public policy, in this case urban green space allocation in low-income communities.
usage_1.example_context: Rivera uses 'network' when discussing how community organizations and city agencies are linked in ways that either facilitate or obstruct equitable green space policy.

usage_2.speaker: Dr. Lena Zhou
usage_2.definition: A computational graph structure composed of nodes and edges used to represent spatial relationships in data, or alternatively a neural network — a layered mathematical model inspired by biological neurons used in machine learning to identify patterns in datasets such as satellite imagery or demographic data.
usage_2.example_context: Zhou uses 'network' when describing her spatial analysis pipeline or the ML model architecture she built to predict green space access scores across city blocks.

ground_truth.explanation: In political science, 'network' refers to real-world relational structures among human and institutional actors that have political agency and shape policy. In computer science, 'network' refers to an abstract mathematical or computational structure (graph or neural network) used for data modeling and analysis. The two usages share a metaphor of interconnection but refer to fundamentally different objects — one social/political, one computational/mathematical.
